cards.when: reducing a many-dimensional covariate vector to one score so treated and control units can be compared, under selection on observables
cards.when_not: treatment is randomised (no score needed); selection is on unobservables (-> IV or DiD); there is no overlap to trim to

alternatives.criterion: few covariates and you want exact comparability
you want protection against a misspecified score
you want to keep the whole sample rather than match

output_key_fields: pscore: the fitted propensity per unit
common_support: the retained overlap region and how many units each arm lost
overlap_diagnostics: score distributions by arm and the minimum/maximum of the common range
auc: discrimination, which should be moderate -- not high
interpretation_traps: a HIGH propensity-score AUC is bad news, not good: near-perfect prediction of treatment means no overlap and nothing to compare
trimming changes the estimand -- the effect is now for the retained overlap population, not the original one, and that must be reported
the score is only as good as the covariates in it; balancing the score does not balance anything omitted from it

cards.method: Nearest-neighbour, caliper, kernel and radius matching
cards.when: constructing a comparison group by pairing treated units with similar controls, when you want a transparent design rather than a regression adjustment
cards.when_not: overlap is poor and matching would discard most of the sample; the covariate set is high dimensional (-> weighting or double ML)

alternatives.criterion: you want to retain the full sample
poor matches must be refused rather than accepted at any distance
you want to use many controls per treated unit for efficiency

output_key_fields: att/atc/ate: the matched effect for the requested estimand
matched_pairs: the pairing, so the design is auditable
n_unmatched: treated units dropped for want of a match inside the caliper
se: standard error, which must account for the matching, not the naive one
interpretation_traps: the naive standard error over matched pairs is WRONG -- matching is not sampling and the estimated score adds variance (-> the bias-corrected estimator)
matching with replacement reuses good controls, which lowers bias and raises variance; without replacement the answer depends on the ORDER units are processed
unmatched treated units silently change the estimand from ATT to ATT-on-the-matchable
sources: Dehejia & Wahba 2002 (Review of Economics and Statistics 84:151)
Imbens & Rubin 2015, Causal Inference for Statistics, Social and Biomedical Sciences

cards.method: Abadie-Imbens bias-corrected matching with valid standard errors
cards.when: you need matching estimates whose standard errors are actually valid, and a correction for the bias that matching on a continuous score leaves behind
cards.when_not: matching is exact so there is no bias to correct; the design is weighting rather than matching

alternatives.criterion: you accept the bias and do not need valid inference
you would rather have double robustness than a bias correction
the outcome model is credible on its own

output_key_fields: att/ate: the bias-corrected estimate
bias_correction: the size of the adjustment, which reveals how poor the matches were
se: the Abadie-Imbens variance, which accounts for matching and for the estimated score
n_matches_used: match multiplicity per treated unit
interpretation_traps: the bootstrap is INVALID for nearest-neighbour matching -- Abadie and Imbens proved it fails, so a bootstrapped standard error here is simply wrong
a large bias correction is a warning that the matches were poor, not a sign the correction worked
matching on an ESTIMATED score adds variance that the naive formula omits entirely
sources: Abadie & Imbens 2008 (Econometrica 76:1537) -- failure of the bootstrap
Abadie & Imbens 2011 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 29:1)

cards.method: Coarsened exact matching and stratified matching
cards.when: you want the balance guarantee of exact matching without its emptiness in continuous covariates, by coarsening first and matching exactly on the bins
cards.when_not: the covariate set is large enough that coarsening leaves every stratum empty; you need a continuous score (-> propensity matching)

alternatives.criterion: many covariates, so exact strata would be empty
all covariates are already discrete and plentiful
you want strata but on one dimension

output_key_fields: weights: CEM weights per unit, zero for unmatched units
strata: the retained strata and their treated/control counts
imbalance_l1: the multivariate L1 imbalance before and after
n_dropped: units in strata lacking both arms
interpretation_traps: coarsening is a bias-variance dial you set BEFORE seeing the outcome; tuning it against the estimate is specification search
the L1 imbalance measure is bounded above by the coarsening itself -- a small value on a coarse grid does not mean the underlying covariates balance
unmatched strata change the estimand, and with many covariates most strata are empty

cards.method: Inverse probability weighting, stabilised weights and doubly-robust AIPW
cards.when: estimating an average effect by reweighting rather than matching, and buying insurance against misspecification by combining the weight model with an outcome model
cards.when_not: overlap is so poor that weights explode; treatment is continuous without a dose-response model

alternatives.criterion: you prefer an explicit paired design
the treatment model is credible and you want simplicity
you want a substitution estimator with the same double robustness

output_key_fields: ate/att: the point estimate for the requested estimand
weights: per-unit weights, stabilised where asked
max_weight, ess: the largest weight and the effective sample size -- the diagnostics that matter
se, conf_int: influence-function based inference
interpretation_traps: a handful of extreme weights can drive the entire estimate; ALWAYS read the effective sample size, which is often a small fraction of n
doubly robust means consistent if EITHER model is right -- it does not mean consistent if both are wrong, and it does not fix poor overlap
stabilised weights fix the variance, not the bias; if the treatment model is wrong, stabilising hides the symptom
sources: Hernan & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If

cards.method: Balance diagnostics: standardised differences, variance ratios and love plots
cards.when: checking whether a matching or weighting design actually achieved comparability, which is the only thing that licenses the causal reading
cards.when_not: the design is randomisation with a large sample, where balance is guaranteed in expectation

alternatives.criterion: the standard, sample-size-free summary
means balance but spread may not
the whole distribution matters, not the first two moments

output_key_fields: smd_before/smd_after: standardised difference per covariate
variance_ratio: treated-to-control variance per covariate
love_plot_data: covariates ordered by post-adjustment imbalance, ready to plot
worst_covariate: the covariate that remains least balanced
interpretation_traps: a t-test of balance is the WRONG instrument -- it conflates imbalance with sample size, so trimming makes it 'pass' by losing power
balancing means says nothing about higher moments or interactions; a design can balance every mean and still compare different populations
balance can only be checked on OBSERVED covariates; it is silent about the ones that drive selection

cards.when: you want a transparent design that uses the whole sample: split on the score into strata, estimate within each, and aggregate
cards.when_not: the score has poor overlap so some strata contain one arm only; you need unit-level pairing

alternatives.criterion: you want explicit pairs rather than blocks
you want a continuous weight rather than blocks
you want exact strata on covariates rather than on the score

output_key_fields: stratum_effects: the effect and count within each stratum
ate/att: the aggregate, weighted by stratum size or by treated count
balance_by_stratum: standardised differences within each stratum
n_strata_dropped: strata lacking one arm
interpretation_traps: five strata is a convention, not a result; the number of strata is a bias-variance choice and the estimate moves with it
a stratum containing only one arm contributes nothing and silently changes the estimand
within-stratum balance must be checked separately -- overall balance can hold while individual strata are badly imbalanced

cards.method: Sensitivity to hidden bias: Rosenbaum bounds and the E-value
cards.when: asking how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to overturn the finding -- the only honest answer to 'but what about omitted variables'
cards.when_not: the design is randomised; the effect is already null, in which case there is nothing to overturn

alternatives.criterion: the design is matched and you want a p-value under bias
you want a single transportable number on the risk-ratio scale
the design is regression with observable selection

output_key_fields: gamma_critical: the odds of differential assignment at which significance is lost
bounds: p-value bounds across the gamma grid
e_value: the minimum confounder association that would explain away the estimate
e_value_ci: the same for the confidence limit, which is the more conservative reading
interpretation_traps: these bound the effect of an unmeasured confounder; they do NOT test whether one exists and cannot
a gamma near 1 means the finding is fragile to very mild hidden bias -- report it, do not bury it
the E-value is on the risk-ratio scale; applying it to a coefficient without converting is meaningless

cards.method: G-computation, standardisation and targeted maximum likelihood
cards.when: estimating a causal effect by modelling the outcome and averaging predictions over the covariate distribution, with a targeting step that restores valid inference
cards.when_not: there is no overlap; the outcome model cannot be fitted credibly and no machine learner helps

alternatives.criterion: you want the same double robustness in an estimating-equation form
the outcome model is credible and you accept model-based inference
the treatment model is the one you trust

output_key_fields: ate/att: the standardised effect
potential_outcomes: mean outcome under each arm, averaged over the covariate distribution
influence_curve_se: inference from the influence function, valid after targeting
initial_vs_targeted: how far the targeting step moved the estimate
interpretation_traps: plain g-computation with a machine-learned outcome model has NO valid standard error -- that is exactly the gap the targeting step exists to close
a large gap between the initial and targeted estimate signals a poorly specified initial model, not a successful correction
the estimand is defined by the covariate distribution you average over; averaging over the treated gives ATT, over everyone gives ATE, and the difference is not cosmetic
sources: van der Laan & Rubin 2006 (International Journal of Biostatistics 2:11)
van der Laan & Rose 2011, Targeted Learning
